question:
Τοπωνύμια πειρατικών και κουρσάρικων ορμητηρίων στην Ανατολική Μεσόγειο (1600-1700)
Research scope: Νέα πραγματική αναζήτηση πηγών για ορμητήρια, αγκυροβόλια και καταφύγια πειρατών και κουρσάρων στην Ανατολική Μεσόγειο, 1600–1700. Αναζήτησε σε όλες τις έντεκα οικογένειες πηγών, περιηγητές, portolans, σύγχρονα κείμενα, αρχεία και μεταγενέστερες μελέτες. Απόκτησε τα προσβάσιμα πραγματικά κείμενα. Για κάθε εύρημα δώσε ιστορικό τοπωνύμιο, σύγχρονη ταύτιση και γεωγραφική θέση μόνο όπου τεκμηριώνονται, χρονολογία, χρήστες, είδος χρήσης, ακριβή πηγή, σελίδα ή φύλλο ή αρχειακή αναφορά, ακριβές απόσπασμα, confidence και verification status. Ξεχώρισε αναφορά πηγής, ερμηνεία και υπόθεση, μεταγενέστερη μελέτη από πρωτογενές τεκμήριο και ορμητήριο από τόπο επιδρομής. Μην μετατρέπεις τη χρονολογία του ερωτήματος σε χρονολογία αχρονολόγητου γεγονότος. Δήλωσε απρόσιτα αρχεία και ανεξέταστο υλικό. Καμία αυτόματη ιστορική επαλήθευση.

source_occurrences.title: Occasioned by the death of Creveliers off Astypalaia: The island's role in the raids by Catholic corsairs during the 17th century

evidence.text:
Occasioned by the death of Creveliers oﬀ Astypalaia:
The island’s role in the raids by Catholic corsairs during the 17th century
Giorgos Koutzakiotis
Between shortly before midnight of the 24th and early morning of the 25th of September 1679, the life of
French corsair Hugues Creveliers, leader of the most important corsair company active in the Aegean sea
in the 1670s, came to an inglorious end oﬀ the coast of Astypalaia, due to the blowing up of his ship by a
member of his crew. The present study takes a closer look at the details of the event and attempts to
portray the role that Astypalaia played in the raids of Catholic privateers against the Ottomans during the
seventeenth century; raids which had become a regular occurrence because of the protracted VenetianOttoman wars. The privileged geographical location of the island made it an ideal base for the corsairs to
launch their attacks against commercial ships following the routes between Alexandria and Constantinople.
At the same time, Astypalaia was an excellent hideout for corsairs, not only because they could ﬁnd provisions there (such as bread, wine, etc.) and stock up with drinking water, but also because the island provided
plenty of safe anchorages. The names of Astypalaia’s havens in French and Italian portolan texts, along with
other information of the time (testimonies about corsair contracts written on the island and marriages
between privateers and local Greek women), attest not only the strong relationship that the corsairs built
with Astypalaia, but also the degree of appropriation of the place by them. In the last part of this study we
examine the role of the bay of Vathy in the corsair raids, since this is most likely where the explosion
of Creveliers’ ship took place. This particular bay has similar traits to other anchorages in the Cycladic
islands where we know that corsairs repaired their ships, since they had built small forts or batteries at the
narrow entrances to these lairs so that no enemy ship could approach. In-situ research conducted by the
author on the south side of the narrow straits of Vathy bay led to the discovery of similar built structures
which seem to be relevant to the frequent corsair presence there.

variations, undoubtedly linked to the ancient name of Phournoi, often coexist with variants of the name
“Phournoi”. ­Conversely, from the 18th century onwards, variants of the name “Phournoi” appear to prevail
among ­cartographers.
The Latin transliteration of the ancient Greek name and its variants closely resemble the byzantine term for the
act of plunder (koursos/kourson), attested as early as the 8th century (Sophocles 1888, s.v. κοῦρσον 687; ­Kriaras
1982, s.v. κούρσο(ν), κούρσος) and correlate with derivatives of the Italian term corsario, loosely ­translated as
“one who has a license to raid” (letter de course), derived from Medieval Latin term cursarius (­“pirate”, from
Latin cursus; Heinz 2007, s.v. cursarius, cursus). The pronounced similarity between the ­numerous versions of
the ancient name of Phournoi and the various terms for loot and corsair in Latin languages and medieval Greek
has fostered a conjectural association in popular consciousness, often leading to the belief that the islands derive
their name from pirate activity. This somewhat arbitrary popular perception, however, does not preclude the
historical possibility that the archipelago of Phournoi was indeed a hub of intense pirate activity in the past.
A series of coastal toponyms documented on maps or utilized in the modern vernacular of Phournoi
are probably the living remnants of pirate activity in the past: Kourniachto (a place for hiding or lurking),
­Kleftolimano (harbor of thieves), Fygou (escape), Fylakio (guard-post), Vardia (shift or guard), Tourkolimnionas
(harbor of the Turks), Pano and Kato Maneta (upper and lower Maneta). Many of these names are commonplace along the Aegean coastline and are also encountered on other islands historically associated with piracy.
However, the two bays designated as Pano and Kato Maneta, situated roughly in the middle of the eastern coast
of the main island of Phournoi, warrant further comment.
It is highly probable that these two bays derived their names from the Zakynthian corsair Eustathios ­(Stathis)
Romanos or Manetas, who, between 1678 and 1684, operated as a pirate in the Aegean Sea while based in Melos,
commanding the only Greek privately owned corsair vessel at the time, most probably handed to him after the
death of its former owner, the Maltese corsair Hugues Creviliers (Krantonelli 1994, 289–91). Early records of
his exploits date back to 1683, when the rector of Tenos reported that Stathis Romanos Manetas had seized the
Venetian consul in Paros, extorting a monopoly over the supply of galette to Venetian fleet vessels. In May 1684,
Admiral Gerolamo Cornaro courted him on behalf of the Venetians, granting him a free pass permit (salvocondotto). Manetas subsequently conducted operations across the Aegean, Ionian and southern Adriatic, either
independently or in collaboration with the Venetians and the Knights of Malta (Krantonelli 1991, 300). At

Ottoman pirates, who were more often referred to as levend or

went out of law and were punished for this reason. The main pirates
are the Christians who appeared in the Mediterranean after the 14th
century. Their aim was to capture booty and captives on a large scale.
The Ottoman Empire regulated and helped develop unregulated
Turkish piracy in the Mediterranean beginning at the end of the 14th
century. The famous Turkish pirate of this period, Kemal captain,
burned a Spanish fleet in Andalusian waters with a pirate fleet
prepared by the Ottoman Empire and plundered the city of Malacca.
By making the island of Djerba a base, it became a dangerous enemy
for Christian Europe. Turgut, Piri, and Murad captains tried to turn the
Mediterranean into a Turkish lake by fighting the Spaniards and
Venetians. Meanwhile, İlyas, İshak, Oruç, and Hızır captains, who
began their piracy in North Africa, launched an attack on the Spaniards
